definition: Great physical beauty, especially of a person
example: The magazine praised the actor's pulchritude but said little about his talent.
origin: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher, meaning “beautiful”.

definition: To make something deliberately unclear or hard to understand
example: The company used dense legal jargon to obfuscate the real cost of the loan.
origin: From Late Latin obfuscare, “to darken”, from ob- “over” and fuscus “dark”.

definition: Relaxed and unworried, showing a casual lack of concern
example: She gave an insouciant shrug and walked into the exam without any notes.
origin: From French insouciant, from in- “not” and soucier “to worry”, ultimately from Latin sollicitare “to disturb”.

definition: Using very few words to say something
example: His laconic reply to my three-page email was a single word: fine.
origin: From Greek Lakonikos, “of Laconia”, the region around Sparta, whose people were famous for their terse speech.

definition: Generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or enemy
example: The champion was magnanimous in victory, praising her opponent's skill and courage.
origin: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus “great” and animus “soul, spirit”.

definition: Not telling the truth; habitually dishonest
example: The mendacious salesman swore the used car had never been in an accident.
origin: From Latin mendax (stem mendac-), meaning “lying”, related to mendum “fault”.

definition: Extremely generous, especially in giving money or gifts
example: A munificent donation from a former student paid for the new library.
origin: From Latin munificus, from munus “gift” and facere “to make”.

definition: Wicked or criminal in a shocking way
example: Police uncovered a nefarious scheme to steal the savings of elderly residents.
origin: From Latin nefarius, from nefas “wrong, crime”, from ne- “not” and fas “divine law”.

definition: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind or feelings
example: Despite hours of pleading, the landlord remained obdurate and refused to lower the rent.
origin: From Latin obduratus, past participle of obdurare “to harden”, from durus “hard”.

definition: Extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources
example: My parsimonious uncle reuses tea bags and never turns on the heating.
origin: From Latin parsimonia “thrift”, from parcere “to spare”.

definition: Very clear, either to see through or to understand
example: Her pellucid explanation made quantum physics seem almost simple to the whole class.
origin: From Latin pellucidus, from perlucere “to shine through”, from per “through” and lucere “to shine”.

definition: Done quickly and carelessly, without real interest or effort
example: The guard gave my bag a perfunctory glance and waved me through.
origin: From Late Latin perfunctorius “careless”, from Latin perfungi “to get through with, discharge”.

definition: Causing serious harm, often slowly and without being noticed
example: The pernicious rumor spread quietly online and eventually ruined her reputation.
origin: From Latin perniciosus, from pernicies “ruin”, from per- “completely” and nex “death”.

definition: Calm and not easily excited or upset
example: The phlegmatic pilot announced the engine trouble as if reading a weather report.
origin: From Greek phlegmatikos, from phlegma “phlegm”, the bodily humor once believed to cause a calm, sluggish temperament.

definition: Complaining in a whining, irritable way
example: The querulous passenger grumbled about the seat, the food, and the delay.
origin: From Latin querulus, from queri “to complain”.

definition: Cheerfully hopeful, especially in a difficult situation
example: Despite falling sales, the founder remains sanguine about the company's future.
origin: From Latin sanguineus “of blood”, from sanguis “blood”; in medieval medicine a temperament ruled by blood was thought to be cheerful.

definition: Using very long words; long-winded
example: The professor's sesquipedalian lectures sent students reaching for their dictionaries.
origin: From Latin sesquipedalis, “a foot and a half long”, a term the poet Horace used to mock overly long words.

definition: Tending to make a person feel sleepy
example: The warm room and the speaker's soporific voice had half the audience nodding off.
origin: From Latin sopor “deep sleep” combined with -ficus “making”, from facere “to make”.

definition: Seeming true or right but actually false
example: The ad relied on the specious claim that expensive vitamins prevent every illness.
origin: From Latin speciosus “beautiful, plausible”, from species “appearance”.

definition: Behaving as if one is better than others
example: The supercilious waiter raised an eyebrow when we ordered the cheapest wine.
origin: From Latin superciliosus, from supercilium “eyebrow”, from super “above” and cilium “eyelid”.

definition: Done secretly to avoid being noticed
example: He took a surreptitious look at his phone during the long meeting.
origin: From Latin surrepticius, from surripere “to seize secretly”, from sub “under” and rapere “to seize”.

definition: Strongly favoring one side of an argument; biased
example: The documentary was so tendentious that it ignored every fact against its case.
origin: From German tendenziös, from Tendenz “tendency”, ultimately from Latin tendere “to stretch”.

definition: Sharp, forceful, and clear in expressing ideas
example: Her trenchant review exposed every weakness in the film's plot.
origin: From Old French trenchant “cutting”, the present participle of trenchier “to cut”.

definition: Insincerely flattering in an oily, overly smooth way
example: The unctuous host praised every guest while clearly angling for donations.
origin: From Medieval Latin unctuosus, from Latin unctus “anointing”, from unguere “to anoint”.

definition: The quality of seeming true or real
example: Real street names and local slang give the novel a strong sense of verisimilitude.
origin: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verus “true” and similis “like”.

definition: To criticize someone using harsh, abusive language
example: Callers phoned the radio show to vituperate the mayor over the tax increase.
origin: From Latin vituperare “to blame”, from vitium “fault” and parare “to prepare”.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is complicated or obscure
example: The lecture on abstruse tax law left most of the audience baffled.
origin: From Latin abstrusus “hidden”, past participle of abstrudere “to conceal”, from ab- “away” and trudere “to push”.

definition: Full of anger, bitterness, and harsh words
example: After an acrimonious divorce, the couple communicated only through their lawyers.
origin: From Latin acrimonia “sharpness”, from acer “sharp”.

definition: Cheerful eagerness and speed in doing something
example: She accepted the job offer with alacrity and started the following Monday.
origin: From Latin alacritas, from alacer “lively, eager”.

definition: Something or someone that is intensely disliked
example: Wasting food was anathema to my grandmother, who grew up during the war.
origin: From Greek anathema, “a thing devoted”, later “a thing devoted to evil”, from anatithenai “to set up”.

definition: Widely told but probably not true
example: The story that he invented the dish by accident is almost certainly apocryphal.
origin: From Greek apokryphos “hidden”, from apokryptein “to hide away”.

definition: Working with great care, effort, and persistence
example: An assiduous researcher, she checked every source twice before publishing.
origin: From Latin assiduus, from assidere “to sit beside, attend to”, from ad “to” and sedere “to sit”.

definition: Eager to fight or start a conflict
example: The president's bellicose speech raised fears of war in the region.
origin: From Latin bellicosus, from bellum “war”.

definition: A harsh, unpleasant mixture of loud sounds
example: A cacophony of car horns and jackhammers greeted us outside the hotel.
origin: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos “bad” and phone “sound”.

definition: Rude, unfriendly, and bad-tempered
example: It would be churlish to refuse such a kind and generous invitation.
origin: From Old English ceorl, “peasant, man of low rank”.

definition: Using many words where fewer would do
example: After ten minutes of circumlocution, the minister still had not answered the question.
origin: From Latin circumlocutio, from circum “around” and loqui “to speak”.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing
example: She presented a cogent argument for moving the company's headquarters to Denver.
origin: From Latin cogere “to drive together, compel”, from co- “together” and agere “to drive”.

definition: Feeling or showing deep regret for doing wrong
example: The contrite teenager apologized and offered to pay for the broken window.
origin: From Latin contritus “ground to pieces”, from conterere “to grind”, from terere “to rub”.

definition: Causing harm or damage, often in a subtle way
example: Lack of sleep has a deleterious effect on both memory and mood.
origin: From Greek deleterios “noxious”, from deleisthai “to hurt”.

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm
example: After a few desultory attempts at conversation, they both returned to their phones.
origin: From Latin desultorius, from desultor, a circus rider who leaped from horse to horse, from desilire “to leap down”.

definition: Overflowing with cheerful energy and excitement
example: The ebullient crowd sang and danced in the streets after the final whistle.
origin: From Latin ebullire “to bubble out”, from e- “out” and bullire “to boil”.

definition: Lively, bubbly, and full of high spirits
example: Her effervescent personality made her the natural host of the morning show.
origin: From Latin effervescere “to boil up”, from ex- “out” and fervescere “to begin to boil”.

definition: Calmness and steady temper, especially under pressure
example: He took the news of the layoffs with remarkable equanimity.
origin: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus “even” and animus “mind”.

definition: Understood by only a small group with special knowledge
example: The forum is full of esoteric debates about vintage synthesizer circuits.
origin: From Greek esoterikos “belonging to an inner circle”, from esotero “more within”, the comparative of eso “within”.

definition: Silly and pointless, often in a self-satisfied way
example: He kept making fatuous remarks while everyone else tried to solve the problem.
origin: From Latin fatuus, meaning “foolish”.

definition: Calm, happy, and peaceful, especially of a past time
example: She often talks about the halcyon days of her childhood by the sea.
origin: From Greek alkyon, “kingfisher”, a bird fabled to calm the sea while it nested around midwinter.

definition: Too great or intense to be put into words
example: Standing at the summit at sunrise, she felt an ineffable sense of peace.
origin: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- “not” and effari “to speak out”.

definition: Having a long-established habit that is unlikely to change
example: An inveterate traveler, he has visited more than ninety countries.
origin: From Latin inveteratus, from inveterare “to make old”, from vetus “old”.

definition: Completely clear and transparent, like still water
example: We could see every pebble at the bottom of the limpid mountain lake.
origin: From Latin limpidus, meaning “clear”.
